name: healthy_start
policy_description: Expand the Healthy Start scheme: raise the weekly voucher value, widen eligibility to all households on Universal Credit with a child under five or a pregnant woman, and let the card be used at convenience stores and market stalls as well as supermarkets, across England.

spec.policy_summary: Expansion of the NHS Healthy Start scheme in England. The weekly prepaid card value rises from £4.25 to £6.50 per child (£8.50 under one), eligibility widens to every household on Universal Credit with a child under five or a pregnant woman regardless of earnings, and the card becomes usable at registered convenience stores and market stalls as well as supermarkets and online grocers, for fruit, vegetables, pulses, milk and infant formula. Delivered through the existing NHS Business Services Authority card and an online application. Intended to improve diet quality and reduce food insecurity in low-income families with young children.

population: Low-income families with children under five

open_questions: Whether take-up improves without proactive outreach, given the current ~60-70% uptake
Whether small retailers will register and stock eligible fresh produce
How the digital-only application affects households without reliable internet or ID documents
outcomes_of_interest: Increase take-up among eligible families who currently miss out
Improve fruit and vegetable intake in low-income families with young children

## Population Relevance Assessment

22 characteristics rated HIGH or MODERATE across 6 categories. Eligibility through Universal Credit is shared background for the proposed sub-groups; the differences below concern take-up and access to eligible foods.

### Geography

| Characteristic | Relevance | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Urban deprived | [High] | Convenience-store registration could expand access, but fresh-produce stocking may limit gains. |
| Suburban deprived | [High] | Poor transport makes participation by nearby retailers especially important. |
| Rural deprived | [High] | Sparse registered retailers and limited online delivery may prevent families using the higher allowance. |
| Urban mixed | [Moderate] | Registered markets may improve choice, though access varies sharply between neighbourhoods. |
| Suburban mixed | [Moderate] | Variable fresh-food access makes retailer participation consequential for some families. |
| Rural mixed | [Moderate] | Distance to registered shops may reduce the usable value of the card. |

Low: Urban affluent; Suburban affluent; Rural affluent.

### Household and Financial Context

| Characteristic | Relevance | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Financially strained | [High] | A higher allowance directly eases food budgets and could increase produce purchases. |
| Unstable cash flow | [High] | Weekly card credit can bridge irregular paydays and protect produce spending. |
| Stable with high overheads | [High] | Removing the earnings limit brings some Universal Credit families into eligibility. |
| Family with children | [High] | Child age determines eligibility and card value; this is largely shared target-population context. |
| Dependent on support | [Moderate] | Applying and reaching registered retailers may require help from others. |

Low: Financially insulated; Adult living alone; Multi-adult houseshare; Retired couple.

### Time, Routine and Domestic Capacity

| Characteristic | Relevance | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Time scarcity | [High] | Limited shopping windows make nearby registered retailers and application time decisive. |
| Erratic routines | [Moderate] | Irregular shopping may favour accessible top-up outlets over planned supermarket trips. |
| Minimal capacity | [Moderate] | Limited equipment can restrict use of some eligible produce and pulses. |
| Limited capacity | [Moderate] | Small storage spaces may constrain purchases of fresh food. |

Low: Rigid routines; Hands-off consumer.

### Emotional and Cognitive Bandwidth

| Characteristic | Relevance | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Digitally excluded | [High] | An online-only application could prevent eligible families receiving any benefit. |
| Neurodivergence, psychological distress and burn-out | [Moderate] | Application demands and shopping environments may impede take-up or card use. |

Low: Socially isolated.

### Diet, Food and Health Needs

| Characteristic | Relevance | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Non-negotiable dietary needs | [Moderate] | Eligible staples may help, but retailer stock may not meet specific dietary requirements. |

Low: Active GLP-1 user; Living with obesity; Past GLP-1 user; Performance diet.

### Ethnicity and Cultural Food Practices

| Characteristic | Relevance | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| South Asian dietary traditions | [Moderate] | Registered shops may not stock preferred eligible vegetables or pulses. |
| Black Caribbean and African dietary traditions | [Moderate] | Registered shops may not stock preferred eligible vegetables or pulses. |
| Eastern European dietary traditions | [Moderate] | Registered shops may not stock preferred eligible produce; application language may add friction. |
| Other culturally specific dietary patterns | [Moderate] | Registered shops may not stock preferred eligible produce. |

Low: None.

Categorical pattern in ethnicity and cultural food practices: all four modifiers are MODERATE because the availability of culturally relevant *eligible* produce at registered retailers determines how useful the card is. Language-related friction is an additional issue for some households, not an assumption about every tradition.

#### 1. Deprived urban families under financial strain

**Why:** The higher allowance could improve produce intake substantially, provided nearby convenience stores register and stock eligible foods.

#### 2. Time-pressed families in deprived suburbs

**Why:** Poor transport and short shopping windows make nearby retailer registration critical; otherwise the increased card value may be difficult to spend.

#### 3. Digitally excluded families in deprived rural areas

**Why:** Online-only applications threaten take-up, while sparse registered shops and limited delivery could also prevent successful applicants using their cards.

#### 4. Time-pressed families with irregular pay

**Why:** Weekly credit could protect fruit and vegetable purchases between paydays, but limited time to apply or shop may blunt the benefit.

#### 5. Overcommitted families in mixed suburbs

**Why:** Removing the earnings limit could benefit Universal Credit families previously excluded despite high fixed costs; local retailer choice will shape use.

#### 6. Deprived urban families with cultural food traditions

**Why:** The card covers produce and pulses, but gains depend on registered retailers stocking eligible foods families actually use.

sections.sg_0:
### Who is impacted

Families with young children in deprived urban areas whose food budgets are under pressure. The combination matters: extra purchasing power helps only if eligible food is affordable and available at retailers they can use [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>“Anyone wishing to do their shop locally in Ingol would be penalized in financial terms.” Inference: a voucher’s value depends on local prices and availability; Preston’s neighbourhoods do not represent every deprived urban area.</badge_detail>

### Benefits and harms

**Likely beneficial for eligible families who receive and can spend the card, but local retail conditions and take-up will determine how much diets improve.** [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“Parents reported that Healthy Start vouchers increased the uptake and variety of fresh fruit and vegetables.” Inference: a higher-value, wider-use card could extend this benefit, but the study examined earlier vouchers.</badge_detail>

- **More room in the budget.** The increase from £4.25 to £6.50 per child each week, alongside wider Universal Credit eligibility, gives qualifying families more money reserved for eligible foods; interviews with low-income parents suggest vouchers can increase children’s fruit and vegetable purchases [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“We bought more fruit and vegetables because we had them.” Inference: greater card value should ease the purchase constraint for recipients; this study did not test the proposed amount or eligibility rules.</badge_detail>
- **More usable outlets.** Adding registered convenience stores and market stalls could let families spend the allowance during local, smaller shopping trips rather than only at existing outlets [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>One parent described buying “milk, or butter or fruit” at a nearby shop; another bought food “a few times a week” as money arrived. Inference: local card acceptance could fit these patterns.</badge_detail>

- **Uneven real value.** The most important second-order risk is that the subsidy benefits retailers without delivering equivalent gains in produce: where participating local shops charge more or stock little suitable food, families may obtain less for the card than at cheaper outlets [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>In one Preston neighbourhood, “shopping locally comes with a huge cost”; the study also found gaps in fruit and vegetable provision. Inference: registered retailers’ prices and stock could dilute the new card’s value.</badge_detail>
- **Eligibility is not receipt.** An online application alone may leave some eligible families unserved; earlier interviews found parents who had applied but stopped receiving vouchers and gave up pursuing them [Analogical: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“Half the sample did not claim their vouchers”; after vouchers stopped, one parent “just gave up”. This concerns administration of earlier paper vouchers, not access to the proposed online application.</badge_detail>

- **Depends on local delivery.** Registration and a reliable range of eligible food will determine whether the new outlets actually reduce shopping friction, rather than simply expanding the list of places where the card might work [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>Preston researchers found “gaps in provision of healthy items” and urged work with retailers on fresh food. Inference: card acceptance alone cannot ensure that eligible produce is on the shelf.</badge_detail>

### Uncertainties

- Whether outreach increases take-up, which nearby retailers register, and what they charge and stock cannot be determined from these studies [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start vouchers low income families uptake value fruit vegetables barriers England” and “Healthy Start prepaid card digital application retailer acceptance market stalls access barriers UK”; no evaluation of this expansion was returned. Track applications, acceptance, stock and prices locally.</badge_detail>
- Consultation with eligible families should test application difficulties and whether card purchases add fruit and vegetables to children’s diets or mainly replace spending families would have made anyway [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start prepaid card digital application retailer acceptance market stalls access barriers UK” and “low income families young children cooking facilities time fresh vegetables food insecurity UK qualitative”; no direct evidence of these outcomes under the proposed design was returned.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Higher card value could improve children’s produce purchases, but take-up and local shops’ prices and stock determine the gain.</step_summary>

sections.sg_5:
### Who is impacted

Deprived urban families with young children whose meals draw on South Asian, Black Caribbean, African, Eastern European or other cultural food traditions. Their shared constraint is not simply finding produce: it is finding eligible ingredients at retailers that accept the card. Language barriers may also affect some households applying online. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined features include urban deprivation, culturally specific ingredients and shopping, and possible language barriers. The policy restricts spending to eligible foods at registered retailers and requires an online application.</badge_detail>

### Benefits and harms

**Likely beneficial for families who enrol, but uneven gains in produce intake depend on which retailers register and what they stock.** [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>“Cost is important and is a prime determinant in food choice, but culture and family food preferences are also important.” Inference: extra credit helps, but its dietary value depends on suitable stock.</badge_detail>

- **Benefits — more purchasing power.** The higher weekly value and wider Universal Credit eligibility should make eligible foods more affordable for families who receive the card, though the subsidy cannot cover the whole food basket. [Inferred: ‘Eating to survive’, 2020]<badge_detail>“Most participants valued eating healthily and had a good understanding of how to prepare and cook healthy meals yet could not afford to do so.” Inference: credit reduces one documented price constraint.</badge_detail>
- **Benefits — familiar shopping routes.** Registering market stalls and convenience stores could let families use the card alongside existing shopping trips, rather than making a separate supermarket trip. [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment?, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>Families of non-British heritage described places to buy specific products cheaply; one parent described using a Polish shop. Inference: registration could make established shopping routes usable for card purchases.</badge_detail>
- **Harms — eligibility is not usability.** The most important second-order risk is that families redirect card spending towards whichever eligible produce registered shops carry, without gaining affordable access to ingredients they would use in familiar meals. Lentils may fit the card; ghee, spices, specific flours or seasonings do not. Plantain and yam depend on stock, while reliance on a specialist shop may matter differently across traditions. [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment?, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>Participants of non-British heritage identified shops selling specific products cheaply and described the dishes made with them. Inference: eligible categories alone do not ensure useful ingredients or acceptance at those shops.</badge_detail>
- **Harms — missed entitlement.** An online-only application may leave some otherwise eligible households without the increased support where language barriers impede navigating the process. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>The subgroup specification identifies language barriers for some households; the policy specifies an online application. Difficulty completing it would prevent use of the card despite eligibility.</badge_detail>
- **Depends on implementation — retail participation.** Produce gains turn on whether culturally relevant shops and stalls register and carry eligible items at usable prices; permitting these outlets is not the same as securing their participation. [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>Researchers found gaps in local fruit and vegetable provision and called for work with retailers on managing fresh food. Inference: extending permitted outlets does not itself establish adequate participating stock.</badge_detail>

### Uncertainties

Take-up, retailer registration and changes in fruit and vegetable intake for these families cannot be estimated from the retrieved evidence. [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start vouchers ethnic minority families uptake language application barriers England” and “Healthy Start vouchers low income families fruit vegetable intake food insecurity financial experience”; no directly relevant evaluation surfaced. Application and purchase data disaggregated by language and ethnicity would help.</badge_detail> Consultation across the traditions described is needed to identify which eligible foods families would buy, which shops they use and whether application support is accessible. [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “low income migrant ethnic minority urban families culturally appropriate food specialist shops fruit vegetables retail access UK” and “ethnic minority low income households cultural cooking traditions ingredients multigenerational food shopping UK”; findings do not establish preferences across all traditions.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Higher card value can help, but produce gains depend on culturally relevant stock at registered retailers.</step_summary>

sections.sg_2:
### Who is impacted

Families in deprived rural areas who are digitally excluded face two distinct hurdles: applying online and finding somewhere practical to spend the card. Neither eligibility nor a higher balance guarantees that eligible food is available locally [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined features: rural deprivation and digital exclusion. The policy requires an online application and spending at registered retailers; its value depends on completing both steps.</badge_detail>

### Benefits and harms

**Mixed — the higher payment could improve diets, but online entry and local retail coverage may prevent families from receiving or using it** [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Digital exclusion obstructs the specified online application; rural location may limit usable registered outlets. Families clearing both hurdles can use the increased payment for eligible food.</badge_detail>

- **More food purchasing power:** For those who obtain the card, the increase from £4.25 to £6.50 per child (£8.50 under one) lowers the out-of-pocket cost of eligible foods; a small study of low-income parents found that Healthy Start vouchers increased the fruit and vegetables they gave children [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children: A qualitative study, 2018]<badge_detail>“Parents reported that Healthy Start vouchers increased the uptake and variety of fresh fruit and vegetables they gave to their children.” Inference: a larger card balance may extend this benefit; rural access was not studied.</badge_detail>
- **More possible outlets:** Allowing registered convenience stores and market stalls could make the card usable on an existing local shopping trip, rather than only at a supermarket, where such outlets are present and registered [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Rural location makes the number of reachable outlets material. The expansion adds convenience stores and market stalls, but only if they register and sell eligible products.</badge_detail>
- **Wider entitlement:** Removing the Universal Credit earnings threshold could include some families with young children or a pregnant household member who previously earned too much to qualify [Reasoning]<badge_detail>The policy extends eligibility to all specified households on Universal Credit regardless of earnings. This benefits those formerly excluded by the earnings threshold, provided they can apply.</badge_detail>

- **Application bottleneck:** An online-only application may leave digitally excluded eligible families without a card at all, making the higher value and wider retail network irrelevant to them [Reasoning]<badge_detail>The subgroup is defined as digitally excluded; the specified delivery requires an online application. Without an accessible way to complete it, eligibility does not become usable support.</badge_detail>
- **Uneven usable value:** The most important second-order risk is that newly eligible families obtain cards but cannot readily spend them on produce if reachable retailers do not register or stock it; repeated shopping trips could then erode the benefit [Analogical: A tale of two cities: A study of access to food, lessons for public health practice, 2010]<badge_detail>In urban Preston, “shopping locally comes with a huge cost” and access outside the area depended on car availability. Rural distances differ; the study illustrates why retailer coverage matters beyond eligibility.</badge_detail>

- **Outreach and assisted application:** Take-up may improve if families can learn about eligibility and apply without managing the online process alone; a voucher study also found that half its small sample were not claiming after applications and payments stopped [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children: A qualitative study, 2018]<badge_detail>“Half the sample did not claim their vouchers”; applicants described vouchers stopping. Inference: resolving access and administrative problems matters for take-up, though this study did not examine digital applications.</badge_detail>

### Uncertainties

- The evidence found does not establish how many digitally excluded rural families can complete this application, or which offline or assisted route they would trust and use [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start voucher uptake application digital exclusion low income families barriers England” and “rural low income families online grocery delivery internet access cooking fresh produce UK”; no directly relevant accounts emerged. Consult affected applicants and local advisers.</badge_detail>
- Local registration, eligible stock and delivery coverage need checking before predicting realised fruit and vegetable intake; consultation should distinguish families who cannot apply from cardholders who cannot spend conveniently [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “deprived rural families food shopping transport convenience shops fresh fruit vegetables access UK” and “rural low income families online grocery delivery internet access cooking fresh produce UK”; results did not establish rural Healthy Start retailer coverage. Map outlets and ask cardholders.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Higher Healthy Start support may improve diets, but digital applications and patchy rural retail could block its use.</step_summary>

sections.sg_4:
### Who is impacted

Universal Credit households with a child under five or a pregnant woman may have relatively stable income but little left for food after high fixed costs. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined features: stable finances with high overheads. Fixed commitments can leave little flexible spending even when income is predictable; eligibility still requires Universal Credit and a qualifying child or pregnancy.</badge_detail> In mixed suburbs, the value of a card usable beyond supermarkets will depend on which nearby shops actually accept it. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined geography is suburban mixed; the policy extends use only to registered retailers. Nearby retailer availability and registration determine where the card can be spent.</badge_detail>

### Benefits and harms

**The likely effect is positive for eligible families who claim, but uneven local retail access could substantially limit the dietary gain.** [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“Parents reported that Healthy Start vouchers increased the uptake and variety of fresh fruit and vegetables.” Inference: higher card value could help, but the study does not test this expansion or suburban access.</badge_detail>

- **Benefits**
  - **New eligibility.** Removing the earnings limit could reach Universal Credit families whose earnings previously excluded them despite high overheads; £6.50 per week per qualifying child also offers more restricted food purchasing power than £4.25. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined features: high fixed costs; policy removes the earnings limit and raises the child rate from £4.25 to £6.50. Eligibility expands, and the nominal card allowance increases, without changing fixed costs.</badge_detail>
  - **More produce.** If families can redeem the card at shops they already use, the extra value could increase fruit and vegetable purchases rather than merely displace existing spending. [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“We bought more fruit and vegetables because we had them.” Inference: increased purchasing is plausible where redemption is convenient; this small study cannot establish the effect of a higher card value.</badge_detail>
- **Harms**
  - **Unequal practical value.** The most important second-order effect is that better-served suburban pockets may gain more than nearby areas with sparse or costly participating shops, reproducing differences in access among equally eligible families. [Inferred: A tale of two cities: A study of access to food, lessons for public health practice, 2010]<badge_detail>“No one local/small shop could compete like for like” on price or availability; shopping outside Ingol depended on car access. Inference: retailer participation alone need not equalise the card’s usable value across mixed suburbs.</badge_detail>
  - **Limited relief.** The card cannot pay high fixed costs or most groceries, so it may improve purchases of eligible foods without resolving a household’s wider budget pressure. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined feature: high overheads. The policy provides a fixed-value card restricted to specified foods, not unrestricted income or support with fixed bills.</badge_detail>
- **Depends on implementation**
  - **Retailer participation.** Registration, produce range and prices at convenience stores and stalls determine whether the new outlets provide a useful alternative to a supermarket trip. [Inferred: A tale of two cities: A study of access to food, lessons for public health practice, 2010]<badge_detail>In Ingol, only one shop sold more than seven vegetable varieties, and local shopping could cost more. Inference: adding eligible outlet types helps only where participating shops offer usable range and value.</badge_detail>
  - **Successful claiming.** Outreach and a workable online application matter: expanding eligibility does not itself put a card in the hands of newly eligible families. [Analogical: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“Half the sample did not claim their vouchers”; some reported vouchers stopping after application. These were earlier paper vouchers, not the proposed online application, but illustrate how entitlement can fail to become use.</badge_detail>

### Uncertainties

- Whether newly eligible families in these suburbs hear about and complete the application—and whether internet or ID requirements obstruct them—needs direct consultation and take-up data. [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start vouchers low income families uptake eligibility application barriers financial pressure food insecurity UK”; no relevant evidence on this subgroup’s digital or ID barriers. Consult eligible families and examine application drop-off.</badge_detail>
- Whether local retailers register and maintain affordable eligible stock needs area-level audits and retailer interviews. [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “small retailers Healthy Start card registration stocking fresh produce market stalls acceptance UK”; no direct evidence on registration or stocking responses to this expansion. Audit outlets, prices and card acceptance across suburban neighbourhoods.</badge_detail>

sections.sg_1:
### Who is impacted

Families with young children in deprived suburbs who have little time for shopping and face poor transport links. When a trip to a larger shop is difficult to fit in, the value of Healthy Start depends unusually heavily on what nearby retailers sell and whether they accept the card [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>Stoke participants described distant supermarkets, taxi costs and less frequent shopping. Inference: narrow shopping windows make those access barriers more consequential for this subgroup.</badge_detail>

### Benefits and harms

**Likely beneficial for eligible families, but local retailer participation will determine how much of the increased allowance becomes usable food.** [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>“Local shops are important in accessing a healthy diet” in deprived Preston areas. Inference: extending card acceptance locally could make the higher allowance usable without an additional journey.</badge_detail>

- **More purchasing power.** For families who obtain and use the card, the rise from £4.25 to £6.50 per child each week reduces the amount they must pay themselves for eligible foods; removing the earnings limit also brings some Universal Credit families into eligibility [Reasoning]<badge_detail>The policy specifies the higher weekly value and wider Universal Credit eligibility. The financial benefit follows only for families meeting those conditions who apply and can spend the allowance.</badge_detail>
- **Trips that fit routines.** If nearby convenience stores register and carry eligible foods, families could buy fruit, vegetables or milk during an existing local trip rather than finding time and transport for a separate supermarket visit [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>One Stoke parent described a single expensive corner shop and walking far for normal shopping. Inference: card acceptance at a suitable nearby shop could remove a separate journey.</badge_detail>

- **Most important second-order effect: unequal usable value.** A nearby registered shop with a narrow or expensive produce range could leave these families getting less food for the same allowance than families able to reach other retailers; the subsidy alone does not change local retail provision [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>In Ingol, “shopping locally comes with a huge cost”; only one local shop stocked a wider fruit and vegetable range. Inference: acceptance without affordable stock limits the card’s purchasing power.</badge_detail>
- **Limited dietary change.** Cheaper ingredients need not become more fruit and vegetables eaten when preparing meals still competes for scarce time; the card does not alter that domestic constraint [Analogical: Cooking Without Thinking, 2021]<badge_detail>“Convenience foods are not deployed simply because there is a lack of time to cook” but help combine cooking and childcare. Bristol parents were studied, not specifically deprived-suburban families; the time constraint transfers.</badge_detail>

- **Retailer implementation.** The access benefit turns on registration, eligible stock, prices and opening hours matching families’ narrow shopping windows—not merely adding convenience stores to the permitted retailer list [Inferred: A tale of two cities, 2010]<badge_detail>The Preston study calls for shops near residents to offer “a healthy range of options”. Inference: permitted card use helps only where an accessible retailer actually participates and stocks suitable food.</badge_detail>

### Uncertainties

- Whether local shops will register, maintain affordable eligible stock, and open when these families can shop needs local retailer mapping and consultation [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “deprived suburban families poor transport local convenience stores fresh produce shopping access” and “Healthy Start prepaid card retailer registration market stalls digital application barriers uptake”; no evidence established future registration or stock responses. Local audits and retailer interviews are needed.</badge_detail>
- The effect of the online application on take-up in this specific group is unknown; ask eligible families about application time and support needs before assuming wider eligibility means wider use [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start voucher low income families uptake barriers value fruit vegetables convenience shops England” and “Healthy Start prepaid card retailer registration market stalls digital application barriers uptake”; no relevant application-experience findings emerged. Interviews with eligible non-applicants are needed.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Higher card value could help, but nearby shops’ participation and produce range determine whether time-pressed families can use it.</step_summary>

sections.sg_3:
### Who is impacted

Families with young children or a pregnant member who face both unstable cash flow and limited time may have little money for produce between payments and little flexibility to complete an application or make a separate shopping trip. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Defined constraints: unstable cash flow and time scarcity. A restricted food credit can bridge a cash shortfall, but obtaining and spending it still takes time.</badge_detail>

### Benefits and harms

**The likely impact is positive for families who obtain and can spend the card, but time costs could leave others without the benefit.** [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“We bought more fruit and vegetables because we had them”; half the small sample did not claim vouchers. Inference: greater value helps users, but access determines reach.</badge_detail>

- **Between-payment protection.** Weekly credit can keep eligible foods affordable when cash runs low, rather than making produce purchases depend entirely on the next payment. [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>Families fitted shopping to their “budget cycle” and sometimes had to forgo it. Inference: weekly restricted credit may preserve some eligible purchases between payments.</badge_detail>
- **More produce to offer.** The higher value could support more fruit and vegetable purchases; a small study of low-income parents reported increased purchases and variety when Healthy Start vouchers were available. [Evidence: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“Parents reported that Healthy Start vouchers increased the uptake and variety of fresh fruit and vegetables they gave to their children.”</badge_detail>

- **Application time cost.** Retaining an online application makes wider eligibility insufficient on its own: a time-pressed eligible parent must still find time to apply and resolve any interruption. [Inferred: Food choices made by low-income households when feeding their pre-school children, 2018]<badge_detail>“It’s the third time it’s happened to us … so I just gave up.” Inference: administrative friction can outweigh perceived value; this study concerned earlier vouchers, not online applications.</badge_detail>
- **Purchase is not consumption.** The key second-order risk is that extra produce does not reliably become meals: limited preparation time leaves cheap, quick alternatives attractive, so purchases alone may overstate dietary gains. [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>Parents described ready meals as “cheap” and quick to “pull … out when you need them.” Inference: restricted preparation time may limit conversion of subsidised ingredients into meals.</badge_detail>

- **Retailer coverage matters.** Registering convenience stores and market stalls could let families use credit during existing trips; the gain depends on those outlets accepting the card and offering suitable produce at useful prices. [Inferred: How do families living in low-income areas engage with the food environment, 2017–2019]<badge_detail>Some families used corner stores for emergency items; others found market produce cheaper. Inference: acceptance in outlets already used may save trips, but coverage and prices determine the gain.</badge_detail>

### Uncertainties

Whether this expansion raises take-up or fruit and vegetable *intake* for families facing both constraints cannot be determined from the retrieved studies. [Gap]<badge_detail>Searched “Healthy Start online application digital exclusion identification documents time barriers parents England qualitative” and “Healthy Start prepaid card small retailers registration acceptance market stalls fresh produce qualitative England”; neither yielded direct evidence on this combined group and expanded scheme.</badge_detail> Consultation should test application time, card use during short shopping trips, retailer acceptance and what happens to purchased produce. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>The defined time scarcity affects applying, shopping and preparation; unstable cash flow affects purchasing. Asking families about each step would distinguish where the policy helps from where it stalls.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Weekly credit may protect produce spending between payments, but application time and usable local retailers determine who benefits.</step_summary>

sections.equity_assessment:
## 
**The expansion is likely to narrow food-purchasing inequality for families who receive and can use the card, but its effect on dietary inequality is mixed because application barriers and local food markets may leave the most constrained families behind.** [Cross-cutting: 6 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>All six analyses identify a potential purchasing benefit conditional on receipt and usable outlets; evidence includes one direct qualitative finding on produce purchases, with distributional conclusions largely inferred or reasoned. SG1, SG2, SG3, SG4, SG5, SG6.</badge_detail>

### Who benefits most

- **Families who can already claim and shop affordably** are best placed to turn the higher balance into fruit and vegetables; earlier qualitative research reports increased purchases and variety among voucher users, but does not establish this expansion’s effects. [Cross-cutting: 3 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Earlier voucher research directly supports increased produce purchases in SG4; SG1 and SG5 extend that finding by inference to the proposed card. SG1, SG4, SG5.</badge_detail>
- **Families with irregular pay** may particularly value weekly food credit between payments, provided a participating shop fits their short shopping windows. This is a reasoned extension of reported shopping patterns, not an observed effect of the expansion. [SG4]<badge_detail>Weekly credit may protect eligible purchases between payments; this was inferred from qualitative accounts of shopping around budget cycles.</badge_detail>

### Who benefits least or is harmed

- **Digitally excluded rural families** could remain eligible but receive nothing if they cannot complete the online application; if they do, distant or unregistered outlets may still make the balance difficult to use. This severe combined risk rests primarily on policy-design reasoning. [SG3]<badge_detail>Online entry and practical redemption are separate hurdles for digitally excluded rural families; both risks were reasoned from the specified delivery route and geography.</badge_detail>
- **Families dependent on nearby shops** may obtain less produce for the same card value where prices are higher or stock is thin. Local-access research supports the concern, but participating retailers’ future prices and stock are unknown. [Cross-cutting: 4 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Unequal usable value recurs in four analyses, supported by inferences from local-shop research rather than evidence on this expansion. SG1, SG2, SG3, SG5.</badge_detail>

### Where groups diverge

- **Adding outlets can remove a journey without making food usable:** time-pressed families may gain from a registered shop on an existing route, while families using specialist shops may still lack familiar eligible ingredients or card acceptance. [Cross-cutting: 3 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Convenient redemption may help short-trip shoppers, whereas acceptance and culturally useful stock must coincide for others; these are inferred or reasoned interactions. SG2, SG4, SG6.</badge_detail>
- **More produce bought need not mean more produce eaten** when childcare and preparation time favour quick alternatives; this matters differently from the financial constraint the card directly reduces. [Cross-cutting: 2 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Time-limited meal preparation may weaken the purchase-to-intake link; one analysis draws on related cooking research analogically and the other infers from parents’ accounts. SG2, SG4.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Higher card value can help, but online entry and local retail conditions determine who gains.</step_summary>

sections.risks_provocations:
## 
### Evidence gaps

- **Who fails to claim, and why?** Application completion, interruptions, language and ID requirements are untested for this design. Track the eligible-to-active-card pathway by area and support need; interview non-applicants. [Gap]<badge_detail>Take-up and application barriers need direct testing, especially for online, time and language constraints. SG1, SG2, SG3, SG4, SG5, SG6.</badge_detail>
- **Where is the balance genuinely spendable?** Registration alone reveals neither produce range nor prices. Audit reachable outlets, card acceptance, opening hours, stock and prices; interview small retailers and stallholders. [Gap]<badge_detail>Future retailer participation, affordable stock and practical coverage remain unknown across all analyses; local audits and retailer interviews would test them. SG1, SG2, SG3, SG4, SG5, SG6.</badge_detail>
- **Does extra spending increase intake?** Link anonymised card-purchase measures with family food diaries or interviews, distinguishing additional produce eaten from displaced spending and unused ingredients. [Gap]<badge_detail>No analysis establishes intake effects under the proposed expansion; purchase substitution and preparation constraints require direct investigation. SG1, SG2, SG4, SG5, SG6.</badge_detail>

### Key assumptions and tensions

- **Can an online-only application increase take-up among eligible families** when those with the greatest access barriers must first overcome them to receive any benefit? [Cross-cutting: 4 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Application friction may prevent receipt; digital exclusion is a design-based risk, while earlier voucher interruptions offer only analogical support. SG1, SG3, SG4, SG6.</badge_detail>
- **Will adding small outlets improve value, or let higher local prices absorb part of the subsidy** for families unable to reach cheaper shops? The analyses establish an access concern, not how retailers will respond to this expansion. [Cross-cutting: 4 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Local price and stock differences could dilute usable value; research supports the access concern, but retailer responses remain untested. SG1, SG2, SG3, SG5.</badge_detail>
- **Is wider Universal Credit eligibility sufficient** for families with high fixed costs when the card cannot cover other groceries or bills? [SG5]<badge_detail>Removing the earnings limit may include households with high overheads, but restricted credit does not resolve those costs; this is policy-design reasoning.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Test the claim-to-intake pathway, especially application losses and the real value of local redemption.</step_summary>

sections.design_improvements:
## 
Challenges against your outcomes of interest: Increase take-up among eligible families who currently miss out; Improve fruit and vegetable intake in low-income families with young children.

### Increase take-up among eligible families who currently miss out

- **Challenge:** Online-only entry may exclude digitally disconnected families and make language or administrative difficulties decisive. [Cross-cutting: 3 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Digital exclusion, language barriers and difficulty resolving interrupted support threaten receipt; the online-specific risks are primarily reasoned. SG1, SG3, SG6.</badge_detail> **Change:** Offer telephone and in-person assisted applications through trusted maternity, health-visiting and community services, with translated guidance and a route to resolve ID or card problems. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Multiple supported routes would address barriers at the point where eligibility must become a working card; their effectiveness should be evaluated.</badge_detail>
- **Challenge:** Removing the earnings threshold does not tell newly eligible or time-pressed families that they qualify. [Cross-cutting: 2 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>New eligibility and limited application time may leave support unclaimed; these are reasoned risks, not measured take-up effects. SG4, SG5.</badge_detail> **Change:** Test proactive, consent-based invitations at relevant Universal Credit, pregnancy and early-years contacts; measure applications, successful activation and sustained use, not awareness alone. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Triggered invitations and pathway measures would test whether outreach reaches eligible non-users without assuming an invitation produces receipt.</badge_detail>

### Improve fruit and vegetable intake in low-income families with young children

- **Challenge:** Permitting convenience stores and stalls does not ensure families can buy affordable produce where they already shop. [Cross-cutting: 4 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Local price, stock and coverage constrain the card’s usable value; the access concern is inferred from earlier research, while registration responses are unknown. SG1, SG2, SG3, SG5.</badge_detail> **Change:** Pilot simple retailer onboarding and produce-stock support in poorly served areas, then publish neighbourhood-level checks of acceptance, range and prices before scaling. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Targeted onboarding paired with monitoring tests whether added outlets improve effective purchasing power rather than outlet counts alone.</badge_detail>
- **Challenge:** Eligible ingredients may not fit familiar meals or limited preparation time, weakening the route from purchase to intake. [Cross-cutting: 3 of 6 sub-groups]<badge_detail>Culturally useful stock and preparation time may determine whether eligible purchases become meals; findings are inferred or analogical, not intake evidence. SG2, SG4, SG6.</badge_detail> **Change:** Co-design retailer stock guidance with families using different food traditions, and explicitly test whether affordable, low-preparation eligible options increase produce eaten. [Reasoning]<badge_detail>Stock guidance and intake testing would address usefulness and consumption without assuming every tradition or household has the same needs.</badge_detail>

<step_summary>Make claiming accessible, then test whether local, usable food purchases become additional fruit and vegetables eaten.</step_summary>
